as_told: In 1953 (or 1979), researchers asked the graduating class at Yale (or Harvard) how many had clear, written goals. Only 3% did. Twenty years later, the 3% with written goals were worth more in money than the other 97% put together.
lesson: Writing down specific goals makes people far more successful than people who do not.
what_happened: No such study took place. The Yale University Library examined records and asked the secretary of the Class of 1953; it found no record, and nobody recalled such a study of that class or any other. The earliest telling found is Mark Victor Hansen's Future Diary (copyright 1983), which says the 1953 Yale class was polled, only three percent had written goals, and twenty years later those few had accomplished more than the other 97 percent. Hansen gives no source.
false_part: The study itself: no Yale class was polled about written goals and followed up twenty years later. The Harvard versions are later retellings; the Matthews summary also calls the Yale/Harvard study an urban myth.

original.quote: There was no relevant record, nor did anyone recall the purported study of the Class of 1953, or of any other class.
It has been determined that no “goals study” of the Class of 1953 actually occurred.

lesson_verdict.why: The only direct test found (Matthews, Dominican University) had 149 participants who completed it, ran for 4 weeks, used self-rated progress and is not peer reviewed. It found that writing goals helped somewhat, which is far from the story's claim of larger lifetime earnings.
